title: What a CAGE 4 Score Measures: An Audit of a Learned Cyber-Defense Benchmark, Its Reference Defenders, and the Tables Built on Them
trick: Redraw the policy seed on fixed environment seeds and read executed actions, not asserted ones: 89% of a CAGE 4 score's spread is the policy's own draw, and silently dropped Restores are still charged.
framing_stripped: Called 'an audit of what a CAGE 4 score measures' with 'a five-item disclosure checklist' and 'the instrument'; it is (a) a reading of the CybORG controller showing that a directive sent to an agent whose previous action is still running is dropped with no error, recorded as Sleep, and charged one point if it is a Restore, measured by switching the two released defenders' own busy checks off (KEEP loses 99.58 points per episode, H-MARL 145.98, both equal to the charge; sec. 6.1) and by delivering a supervisory rule's Restores 'held' (only at idle agents) rather than 'fired' (Table 4); (b) a one-way random-effects decomposition of 100 paired episodes times 4-6 policy sampling seeds, putting 88.9% of KEEP's per-episode outcome variance at the stock adversary on the policy's own sampling draw, which the challenge's evaluation script never seeds (sec. 5); (c) KEEP retrained from scratch with and without the busy check on four paired seeds, with the check-on arm continued to two thousand updates on three seeds against the released checkpoint's reproduction interval (sec. 6.3); (d) two recovery-precision criteria scored on the same Restores (45.6% vs 71.6% for KEEP; sec. 7); and (e) five published comparison tables read against four disclosure axes, none stating all four (Table 10).
method_equations: Reproduction (sec. 2): KEEP's released checkpoint scores $-191.34$ with standard error $3.54$ over four policy sampling seeds on the same 100 environment seeds, a $t$ interval with three degrees of freedom $[-202.61, -180.07]$ containing the published $-193.68$; H-MARL Expert $-131.34$, s.e. $2.91$, $[-140.61, -122.08]$ containing the authors' $-129.53$ and Trident's $-132.63$ (Table 2); both intervals are about twenty points wide, 'four times the gap between the leaderboard's first and second entries (4.65 points)'. The drop (sec. 4.1): at every step the controller stores a directive $a$ asserted for agent $g$ only if $\mathrm{actions\_in\_progress}[g] = \mathrm{None}$ ('There is no else branch'); otherwise it is dropped, the agent's success flag reads IN_PROGRESS and the record shows Sleep. Action durations: Restore 5 steps, Remove 3, Analyse and DeployDecoy 2. The reward adds an action-cost term summed over the directives the caller supplied; Restore is the only blue action with a cost, $c_{\mathrm{Restore}} = 1$ point, charged whether the Restore runs or is dropped. Execution match (sec. 4.2): an intervention asserted at step $t$ for an action of duration $d$ counts as executed iff the step record shows the same agent executing the same action on the same host at step $t + d - 1$. Observed: fired at whatever agent owns the host, $60.5\%$ of the O1 rule's interventions execute on KEEP and $35.8\%$ on H-MARL, against busy shares of $38.5\%$ and $52.9\%$ of agent-steps; held, $99.0\%$ and $98.9\%$ (Figure 1a). Charge/rest split (sec. 4.2, Table 4): for paired arms $A$ (held) and $B$ (fired) on the same 100 environment seeds, $$\Delta = \bar{R}_A - \bar{R}_B, \qquad C = c_{\mathrm{Restore}} \bigl( n^{\mathrm{Restore}}_B - n^{\mathrm{Restore}}_A \bigr), \qquad \mathrm{rest} = \Delta - C,$$ where $\bar{R}$ is the mean episode return and $n^{\mathrm{Restore}}$ the Restores per episode passed to the controller, executed or dropped, read from the step records; each of $\Delta$ and rest carries a 95% percentile bootstrap interval over episodes (10,000 resamples) and a win count. Observed: KEEP stock $\Delta = 25.3$ $[15.6, 35.2]$, 77 of 100, $C = 11.9$, rest $13.4$ $[4.0, 23.0]$; KEEP under Wrecker $\Delta = 172.7$ $[133.8, 212.2]$, $C = 11.8$, rest $160.9$; H-MARL stock $27.6$ $[21.3, 33.8]$, $C = 20.6$, rest $7.0$ $[1.1, 12.9]$; H-MARL Wrecker $316.3$, $C = 20.9$, rest $295.3$ (Table 4). Check ablation (sec. 6.1, Table 6): KEEP with its busy check off scores $-286.90$ vs $-187.32$, cost $99.58$ $[82.74, 115.41]$, 92 of 100; Restores passed rise from $77.46$ to $180.91$ per episode, $102.58$ of them to busy agents; charge $103.45$ $[98.75, 108.22]$, rest $-3.87$ $[-19.49, 10.55]$; across nine adversaries the cost is $81.79$ to $155.05$ and the charge $60.4\%$ to $106.9\%$ of it. H-MARL with its mask off: cost $145.98$ $[142.03, 149.97]$, rest $0.00$ on every episode, executed actions identical on 100 of 100 episodes. Variance decomposition (sec. 5, App. A): let $Y_{ij}$ be the return on environment seed $i \in \{0, \ldots, 99\}$ under policy sampling seed $j \in \{1, \ldots, J\}$ ($J = 4$ at stock, $6$ under Wrecker), modelled as $Y_{ij} = \mu + \alpha_i + \varepsilon_{ij}$ with $\alpha_i$ the scenario (episode) effect and $\varepsilon_{ij}$ the closed-loop response to the policy's draw; $$\hat{\sigma}_w^2 = \frac{1}{I(J-1)} \sum_{i=1}^{I} \sum_{j=1}^{J} \bigl( Y_{ij} - \bar{Y}_{i\cdot} \bigr)^2, \qquad \hat{\sigma}_b^2 = \mathrm{Var}_i\bigl( \bar{Y}_{i\cdot} \bigr) - \frac{\hat{\sigma}_w^2}{J}, \qquad \hat{\rho} = \frac{\hat{\sigma}_w^2}{\hat{\sigma}_w^2 + \hat{\sigma}_b^2},$$ with $I = 100$ and a bootstrap over episodes for the interval on $\hat{\rho}$ (the sampling share). Observed for KEEP: stock $\hat{\sigma}_w = 59.39$, $\hat{\sigma}_b = 21.03$, $\hat{\rho} = 88.9\%$ $[71.6\%, 99.8\%]$; Wrecker $\hat{\sigma}_w = 320.96$, $\hat{\sigma}_b = 41.12$, $\hat{\rho} = 98.4\%$ $[92.7\%, 100.0\%]$. H-MARL: $83.1\%$ at stock over six draws $[74.3\%, 91.7\%]$, $90.7\%$ under Wrecker $[84.7\%, 97.2\%]$. Standard error of a one-seed 100-episode mean, $\sqrt{\hat{\sigma}_w^2 + \hat{\sigma}_b^2} / \sqrt{100}$: about $6.3$ points at stock and $32.4$ under Wrecker. Heavy tail: widest single episode has sampling sd $335.4$ (stock) and $625.5$ (Wrecker), median episode $36.5$ and $316.7$; without the five widest episodes $\hat{\rho} = 72.0\%$ and $96.7\%$. Null band: per-episode difference between two identical KEEP draws has sd $62.1$ to $101.1$ points; the widest realised gap between identical draws is $14.9$ points at stock ($89.3$ under Wrecker), the most lopsided pair has the better draw ahead on 66 of 100. Sampling mode: the same KEEP checkpoint scores $-552.22$ greedy (sd $343.75$) vs $-187.32$ sampled, a factor of $2.95$; mode is undisclosed in every published number. Restore charge share: KEEP passes $77.46$ Restores per episode at stock, charge $= 41.4\%$ of its loss; H-MARL $37.20$, $27.3\%$; the 50.89-point gap between the two defenders contains $40.3$ points of charge difference. Continuation decomposition (sec. 5): three training seeds times three evaluation draws under Wrecker Q32, training seed as factor, between-seed sd of seed means $98.1$ vs within-seed sd across draws $31.5$, training seed accounts for $90.4\%$ of the variance of a draw's paired mean, permutation $p = 0.004$; under Wrecker itself within-seed $45.3$ exceeds between-seed $42.0$, $p = 0.127$. Training (sec. 6.3, Tables 7-8): four paired seeds 4101-4104, arms F (check on) and N (check off), identical initial weights and scenario draws, 5 episodes of 500 steps per update; at 100 updates N leads by $454.4$ to $1654.0$ points scored check-on, from 200 updates F leads in all four seeds by $62.6$ to $460.0$ (12 of 12 paired intervals exclude zero; sign test across four seeds $p = 0.125$); at 400 updates means $-457.8$ (F) vs $-707.6$ (N). F continued to 2000 updates on seeds 4101, 4102, 4103: four-draw means $-316.72$ $[-339.08, -294.35]$, $-218.71$ $[-234.04, -203.38]$, $-189.97$ $[-192.39, -187.56]$ vs released $-191.34$ $[-202.61, -180.07]$: spread across training seeds $126.7$ points vs a released reproduction interval $22.5$ points wide. Precision (sec. 7, Table 9): ground-truth criterion counts a Restore correct if the host held a red session on the step before the Restore completed; evidence criterion counts it correct if the host was in the defender's latched flagged set. KEEP Restores: $45.6\%$ ground truth vs $71.6\%$ evidence, Removes $24.1\%$, pooled $33.3\%$; prevalence $18.9\%$ of owned host-steps. The O1 rule arm scores $65.2\%$ on KEEP's own criterion yet fired trails KEEP by $332.97$ points $[-354.6, -311.2]$ (1 of 100), of which $364.4$ is extra charge, and held is $-5.5$ $[-21.3, 10.1]$. The latched set flags $34.5\%$ of owned host-steps, $27.9\%$ of them carry a red session against $20.1\%$ base rate (lift $1.39\times$), recall $48.0\%$.
load_bearing_assumption: That the within-episode component of the decomposition is 'the policy's own sampling draw' and nothing else, so that $88.9\%$ can be read as how much of a CAGE 4 score is the defender's stochasticity rather than the scenario. The paper's own text qualifies this twice: 'the within component is the closed-loop response to the policy's draw, red and green included, and not run-to-run noise' (sec. 5), and in the limitations, 'the two harnesses reseed different generators with the policy seed, so the two defenders' sampling shares are not measured on the same footing' (sec. 10) — the KEEP harness reseeds only torch while the H-MARL harness reseeds torch, numpy and Python's random. The decomposition has two factors, environment seed and policy seed, and everything the scripted red and green agents do differently once the policy's first sampled action differs is booked to the policy. No arm holds the policy's action sequence fixed and redraws the adversary, so 'who moved' is attributed to two parties where there are at least four (policy, red, green, scenario). Second, that KEEP under the released evaluation protocol (sampling mode, stock FiniteStateRedAgent, 100 episodes) is representative of leaderboard entries: the four entries above KEEP released no code or checkpoint, so 'if the leading entries' scores carry sampling noise like KEEP's (the leaderboard does not say)' (sec. 5) is a conditional the paper cannot discharge. Third, for the training result, that the busy check as a package (skip the step, book busy-time rewards to the next decision, discount per decision, never sample or be charged while busy) is what the paired seeds measure; the paper says 'the mechanism is read from the code and not measured' and the separating arm 'is future work' (sec. 6.4).
weakest_component: The headline $88.9\%$ rests on four policy-seed replicates per episode (six under Wrecker) with a bootstrap interval of $[71.6\%, 99.8\%]$, and the paper documents that the share is carried by a tail: 'the within-episode spread is heavy-tailed and the share is carried by a few episodes', 'without the five widest episodes the share is $72.0\%$ at stock' (sec. 5). The H-MARL first four draws gave $88.9\%$ 'the same as KEEP's to the printed digit, with draw means closer together than a share that high allows ($p = 0.012$)', which moved to $83.1\%$ over six draws, so the estimator is visibly unstable at $J = 4$. Next: (1) the decomposition cannot separate the policy's draw from red's and green's closed-loop response (see load_bearing_assumption), so the lane's attribution question is half-answered; (2) the two defenders are reseeded through different generators, so the KEEP-vs-H-MARL share comparison is not on one footing by the authors' own statement; (3) the training result is four paired seeds for the crossing (exact sign test $p = 0.125$) and three seeds for the continuation, two of them 'still moving when the budget stops it', so the 126.7-point seed spread may be partly a spread in climb rate; (4) the drop's cost on a policy that cannot see the flag is never measured on such a policy — both released defenders read the flag, so the ablation switches off a check the policy was trained with, and 'we did not run an agent on the documented observation itself' (sec. 10); the charge accounting on supervised arms also 'misses a defender's own Restore still running when an episode ends, at most one per agent' (App. A), which is why the H-MARL stock rest of 7.0 is 'not separated from zero'; (5) the five-table audit is a reading of papers, with two open questions the authors 'have not asked' the other groups (ACDZero's sd a third of the measured one; Trident's checkpoint recipe differing from its text), so the audit of others is partly a list of unresolved discrepancies; (6) one environment, two defenders, CPU-only, and the paper's own first scoring of precision was wrong by a capture-timing error it reports ('A correction', sec. 7).
regime: Environment: CybORG / CAGE Challenge 4 template at revision 8c3c50ca54b1 (2025-10-27); enterprise scenario, five blue agents, 500-step episodes; every arm is 100 paired episodes on environment seeds 0-99 (sec. 2). Defenders: KEEP (graph-network PPO; released checkpoint 476,167 actor parameters, trainer as shipped builds 459,783; five checkpoints of 3,536,882 bytes) and H-MARL Expert (hierarchical PPO; fifteen policy files), run in two Docker images because their dependency sets are incompatible (App. A, Table 11). Adversaries: stock FiniteStateRedAgent; Wrecker (hand-specified in Trident's planner schema, six of eight transition rows changed, host-state priority list with 64% weight on hosts red already holds root; Table 1); a ladder ConvOnly, Wrecker Q04/Q16/Q32/Q48; eight heuristic Trident adversaries (Table 6). Score scale: $-6592.68$ (do nothing) to $-22$ (best single episode); KEEP $-187.32$ stock and $-1115.65$ under Wrecker; H-MARL $-136.43$ and $-842.76$. Policy seeds: 4 at stock and 6 under Wrecker for KEEP; H-MARL 4 seeds of the authors' evaluator plus 6 harness draws. Supervisory rules O1, O2, O2f and rule defenders R2, R2d, R4tn, RT (App. A). Training: KEEP from scratch, 4 paired training seeds 4101-4104, 400 updates each, 5 episodes per update (the five the shipped learner reads of 25 generated), check-on arm continued to 2000 updates on 3 seeds, scored every hundredth checkpoint with 4 policy draws at the endpoint; two controls (fixed-layout seeded S on one seed; read-all R on two seeds). Compute: CPU only ('the CPU wheel index for torch'; 'Retraining needs the patched trainer and days of CPU per seed', App. A); no GPU hours or dollar cost stated. Statistics: 95% percentile bootstrap over episodes (10,000 resamples), exact sign tests, $t$ intervals over seeds, permutation test over nine draw means. Artifact: github jrice-ai/cage at tag arxiv-v1, traces and checkpoints on Zenodo (App. A). Date: arXiv 2026-11-10 v1 (cs.CR, cs.LG); venue not stated; the paper states it was drafted with an LLM assistant from a ledger of measured values (AI Disclosure Statement).
information_asymmetry: (1) Policy seed at the harness vs none at the leaderboard. The quantity that sets most of a score's spread, the policy's sampling draw, exists in torch's generator and is never fixed or recorded by the challenge's script: 'the evaluation seeds the environment but not policy sampling, so one command run twice on the same seeds returns different scores' (sec. 5). A leaderboard mean is one draw with s.e. about 6.3 points, 'no leaderboard carries it', and the four entries above KEEP released nothing. (2) Two-factor decomposition vs per-party attribution. The factors are environment seed and policy seed; red's and green's realised actions exist step by step in the paper's own record but are never a third factor, so the $88.9\%$ is 'the closed-loop response to the policy's draw, red and green included'. Replaying the policy's executed actions from the record while redrawing red would split that share; the traces to do it are released. (3) Directives asserted vs actions executed. The simulator knows both; the challenge's record keeps only the second, 'each dropped directive shown as a Sleep', and an agent on the documented observation sees neither the busy flag nor the charge, so its training reward includes 'a credit-assignment cost during training that we name and have not measured' (sec. 4.4). (4) Per-step reward and true state in the simulator vs per-episode totals in the record (Tier C): 'no decision can be scored from what the script writes', so both precision criteria (45.6% vs 71.6%) are reconstructions. (5) Training seed vs evaluation draw: the training seed accounts for 90.4% of a continuation's paired-mean variance under one adversary and is inseparable from the draw under another, while every published retrain is one seed, one draw. For the lane: the leftover is the per-party split of the within-episode component, on public traces.
occupies: Published: that the CybORG controller in CAGE 4 silently drops a directive asserted at a busy agent, records it as Sleep and charges one point for a dropped Restore, with the busy flag absent from the documented vector observation; that both released defenders' own busy checks are worth exactly their charge at evaluation (KEEP 99.58 points, H-MARL 145.98 with executed actions unchanged step for step) and that held delivery of a supervisory rule is worth 25.3/27.6 points at stock and 172.7/316.3 under an impact-focused adversary; the one-way random-effects decomposition putting 88.9% (stock) and 98.4% (Wrecker) of KEEP's per-episode outcome variance on the policy's sampling draw, the 6.3-point standard error of a one-seed 100-episode mean, and the null band between identical draws (up to 14.9 points, 66 of 100 episodes); that the Restore charge is 41.4% of KEEP's loss and 40.3 of the 50.89 points between the two reference defenders; the paired retraining showing KEEP without its busy check ahead at 100 updates and behind from 200 on in all four seeds, and a 126.7-point spread across three training seeds at 2000 updates against a 22.5-point sampling interval; two recovery-precision criteria giving 45.6% vs 71.6% on the same Restores and a 65.2%-precision rule that loses by 332.97 points fired; the reading of five comparison tables against four disclosure axes and the five-item checklist; the pinned reproduction intervals; the instrument, patches, traces and checkpoints. Not claimed and left open: the per-party (policy / red / green / scenario) split of the within-episode variance; the sampling noise of any leaderboard entry above fifth; the cost of the drop on an agent that cannot see the flag; the training arm that keeps the check but credits busy-time rewards per tick; whether Cyberwheel's controller shares the drop; anything about a human supervisor or a real network.

neighbors.title: CybORG++: An Enhanced Gym for the Development of Autonomous Cyber Agents
neighbors.trick: Reimplement the CAGE 2 CybORG simulator with its bugs fixed and a lightweight MiniCAGE variant up to 1000x faster, documenting the original's invalid actions, inconsistent reward and reduced observation visibility; this paper calls it the closest prior audit and notes CAGE 2's one-step actions mean 'the defect catalog of Emerson et al. could not have contained' the duration-based drop (sec. 4.4, sec. 10).

neighbors.title: Automated Cyber Defense with Generalizable Graph-based Reinforcement Learning Agents
neighbors.trick: Represent the network as an attributed graph and train a PPO policy whose actions are graph edits, so the defender transfers zero-shot to unseen topologies and adversaries; this is KEEP, the first reference defender audited here, whose released checkpoint reproduces at $-191.34$ and whose shipped trainer 'never seeds its workers, replays the same scenario draws every update, and learns from five of the twenty-five episodes each update generates' (Contributions).

neighbors.title: ACDZero: MCTS Agent for Mastering Automated Cyber Defense
neighbors.trick: Guide Monte Carlo tree search with graph-neural-network embeddings and learned priors over graph-edit actions to plan cyber defense in CAGE 4 with fewer samples than model-free RL; audited here as one of the five tables, reporting a KEEP baseline 'the leaderboard number to the digit' with an sd 'a third of the checkpoint's across-episode sd', an ablation row equal to the baseline row, and a recovery precision 'with the criterion unstated' (Table 10, sec. 8).

neighbors.title: Trident: How to Break Deep Reinforcement Learning Cyber Defenses (Agentic)
neighbors.trick: Train a 7B LLM planner with verifiable rewards to write executable red-team Python policies against live DRL defenders in CAGE 4 and CyberWheel, cutting defensive performance by an average of 522% against static reds; this paper borrows its planner schema to hand-specify the Wrecker adversary, runs its eight heuristic adversaries, credits it as the only table stating a run-to-run spread, and finds its retrained-KEEP checkpoint records a different recipe from its text (sec. 2, Table 6, sec. 8).

neighbors.title: No One Architecture Fits All: A Cross-Environment Evaluation of Hierarchical Red Team Agents
neighbors.trick: Compare RL-planner/RL-executor and LLM-planner/LLM-executor red teams across CAGE 4 and two Cyberwheel scales under one disruption metric and find the winner inverts with environment size; the fifth audited table, credited as the only one 'stating its criterion, excluding the reward from it and recomputing its numbers from its own traces', while omitting dispersion, seeds and which H-MARL artifact it ran, and its executors 'act every step' without saying whether they keep the busy check (sec. 4.4, sec. 8).

theme_fit.why: a benchmark-validity audit whose central instrument is variance attribution to who moved (policy draw vs scenario) on a sequential-decision benchmark, with the reported mean shown to be one unseeded draw and five comparison tables shown to omit artifact, sampling, criterion and adversary; the per-party split it leaves undone (policy / red / green) is the lane's attribution question stated in the lane sentence, and the instrument and traces are public

sec. 6 turns a wrapper's busy check into a measured credit-assignment choice (skip the step and book busy-time rewards to the next decision vs every tick a transition) with a crossing at 200 updates in four paired seeds, and names the separating arm (per-tick crediting) as future work; a semi-MDP credit question, but on a cyber simulator with CPU-only PPO and no LLM agent

shape match only: a simulator that silently violates its documented contract (drops directives, charges for them) and a policy that exploits an undocumented flag is the lane's 'silent trade' pattern, but the simulator is a network emulator, not a physics engine, and no re-simulation under a reference is involved
no serving, rollout or cost-structure content; compute is 'days of CPU per seed' and not costed further
no context, memory or handoff content

limitations_as_complaints: My variance decomposition says 88.9% of the score is 'the policy's own sampling', but the within-episode component is 'the closed-loop response to the policy's draw, red and green included' (sec. 5), I never hold the policy's actions fixed and redraw the adversary, and my two defenders are not even reseeded the same way: 'the two harnesses reseed different generators with the policy seed, so the two defenders' sampling shares are not measured on the same footing' (sec. 10) — so I cannot say which party's draw moved the outcome, only that it was not the scenario.

I measured the silent drop only where it does not bite: 'its cost on the policies themselves is measured by switching that check off (Section 6), an ablation of each wrapper and no measurement of an agent built without one ... we did not run an agent on the documented observation itself' (sec. 10), and the training-time cost of being rewarded and charged for directives the simulator never ran is 'a credit-assignment cost during training that we name and have not measured' (sec. 4.4).

My training result is a package I cannot unpack: 'the mechanism is read from the code and not measured. A trainer that kept the check and credited the rewards earned while busy to the action that earned them, discounting per tick, would separate the credit assignment from the check itself, and that arm is future work' (sec. 6.4); it rests on four paired seeds (sign test $p = 0.125$) and three continuations, two of which are 'still moving when the budget stops it' (sec. 6.3), at 'days of CPU per seed' (App. A).
